audio_technical_evidence.final_audio_transcript: This wood frog can survive ice forming inside its body. How do its cells survive? In interior Alaska, winter survival starts before the first freeze. The frogs build up urea. Then, as freezing begins, their livers turn stored glycogen into glucose, sugar. Together, these substances limit ice formation and water loss from cells. They help the frog tolerate freezing without stopping it completely. In one experiment, researchers repeatedly froze and thawed, winter-prepared Alaskan wood frogs, finally reaching minus 8 degrees Celsius. All five frogs checked for survival, recovered, and stayed healthy for seven weeks. These were winter-conditioned Alaskan frogs. Not every frog can do this. Their winter strategy — protect living cells while part of the body freezes.
